name: Blocked credits — section 17(5)
definition: Section 17(5) opens with a non obstante clause overriding section 16(1) and section 18(1), and then lists supplies on which input tax credit shall not be available at all. In the source held locally the list is: motor vehicles for transport of persons seating not more than thirteen including the driver; vessels and aircraft; general insurance, servicing, repair and maintenance of those conveyances; food and beverages and a group of listed goods and services; club and fitness centre membership; employee vacation travel benefits; works contract services for construction of immovable property; goods or services for own-account construction of immovable property; supplies taxed under the composition levy; supplies received by a non-resident taxable person; goods or services used for personal consumption; goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off, gifted or given as free samples; and tax paid under the demand and detention provisions. Several entries carry their own exceptions.
why_it_exists: Some inputs are consumed as final consumption rather than passed into a taxable supply, and some are too easily reclassified as business use. Rather than police that case by case, the Act blocks the class. The block is absolute for the class and is not softened by proving business use — s.17(5)(d) says so in terms, blocking own-account construction 'including when such goods or services or both are used in the course or furtherance of business'.
inputs: the nature of the inward supply
the use to which it is put
for conveyances, the approved seating capacity and the use exception claimed
for construction, whether the asset is immovable property and whether it is plant and machinery
outputs: credit blocked, naming the clause of s.17(5)
or an exception within that clause satisfied, so credit survives
preconditions: credit would otherwise be available under s.16(1) or s.18(1)
common_mistakes: claiming credit on a blocked item because it was genuinely used in business — business use does not defeat the block
reading s.17(5) as a restriction to be apportioned; it is an availability bar, not a proportion
treating the s.17(5)(a) exceptions as available to any registered person, when they apply only to the named taxable supplies
treating 'plant and machinery' as everything capitalised; the Explanation excludes land, buildings, civil structures, telecommunication towers and pipelines laid outside the factory
legal_references: CGST Act 2017, s.17(5) and the Explanations to s.17
icai_references: NOT APPLICABLE — blocked credit is a tax availability question; the accounting consequence is that the tax becomes part of cost
evidence_required: the description of the goods or services on the inward document
for conveyances, approved seating capacity and registration particulars
for construction, whether the resulting asset is immovable property and whether it was capitalised
confidence_factors: weak when the invoice description is generic and the blocked category cannot be ruled in or out
an AI that claims a blocked credit creates a real liability for the business — this list is scored strict, and an unresolved description is a clarification, never a claim
UNKNOWN — source is the Act as updated 31-08-2021; later amendments not held locally
CONFLICT — the second locally held source blocks a further class (corporate social responsibility) and states clause (i) differently; see GST-ITC-BLOCKED-17-5-FA and GST-ITC-BLOCKED-17-5-I
validation_checks: no claimed credit falls in any clause of s.17(5) without a stated exception
where an exception is claimed, the exact statutory use is named and evidenced
the s.17 'plant and machinery' Explanation is applied before treating any construction input as creditable
examples: a trading company buys a five-seat car for its director — s.17(5)(a) blocks the credit, and no exception applies because the company does not sell cars, carry passengers or teach driving
counterexamples: a driving school buys the same car to teach driving — the clause (C) exception applies and the credit survives
